body:
The most useful thing the objection and the rival do together is refuse the original account's ranked order of operations: memory-gap first, avoidance second, remedy third. Both argue that this ranking is not forced by the material, and I think they're right about the forcing but not about what follows. So my contribution is to sort the three readings by what they actually disagree about, and to name which disagreements the material can and cannot settle.

There are three readings on the table, but they are not three candidates for one slot. The memory-gap reading (agreements drift because nobody records them) and the scope-ambiguity reading (agreements were never univocal, because 'dishes' and 'this week' have no fixed referent) are both answers to the question 'why do later disagreements arise?' They differ in mechanism, not in domain, and they are compatible: a household can both forget and be ambiguous. The rival makes this point explicitly. The avoidance-as-central reading (the third element in the problem statement is load-bearing, not symptomatic) is an answer to a different question — 'why is the conversation stuck rather than merely repeated?' — and it can be true alongside either of the first two. The objection treats it as a rival to the memory reading, but that's the wrong shape: avoidance being the mechanism by which the household stopped being able to talk is not incompatible with agreements being forgotten or ambiguous.

What this means is that the objection's proposed test — watch whether 'what was agreed' disputes fall after a record is introduced — is not the discriminator it claims to be. I agree with the objection's own diagnosis of why it isn't: it can fall for memorial reasons, fail to fall for normative reasons, and either outcome is readable as supporting the memory reading. But the objection uses that weakness to argue for a specific reordering (avoidance-first, record-optional). That reordering doesn't follow. If the readings are compatible rather than rival, holding them side by side is not a way of suspending judgment until one wins; it's the correct description of what the material supports.

The rival's concrete probe — ask each flatmate separately what they thought a past agreement meant — is the most interesting move across the three pieces, and I want to credit the rival for stating its weakness in advance. Recollection is exactly what's in dispute, so the probe returns current reports, not past agreements. But that doesn't make it useless. It changes what it's a probe of. If the reports cluster around scope, recurrence or timing when asked separately, that's evidence about the shape of the current disagreement — which is compatible with either the memory or the ambiguity reading, but incompatible with the standing-negotiation reading, because standing-negotiation predicts that reports will not cluster around task-features at all. A non-clustering result leaves both the memory and ambiguity readings alive and gives the standing reading no special support. Non-clustering is not evidence for standing-negotiation, only against the prediction that the disputes are about task-features. The rival's commitments already flag that non-clustering shouldn't be scored as victory for whichever reading the observer favored, and I'd sharpen it: non-clustering tells you almost nothing, and the probe's main value is prophylactic — it prevents writing a record before knowing whether the disputes even have a task-shape.

What I would actually distinguish, then, is not three readings but two questions that the material does and does not license asking. Question one: what mechanism produces later disagreements about the same words? The material supports multiple answers and does not rank them. Question two: what would 'settle' look like? The objection names an answer the original account adopts without defending — a drop in 'what was agreed' disputes — and it's worth saying that no answer to question two is implied by any answer to question one. A record could settle task disputes without touching standing disputes, and still be an improvement if task disputes were the ones costing the household the most.

On the avoidant friend, both the objection and the rival are right that the original account inverted its own ranking: it flagged the one-to-one approach as most contestable while treating it as a supplementary move, when it's the move most responsive to the stated third element. The rival's framing — 'I want to hear your view of the group conversations' rather than 'I want to ask why you avoid them' — is a small, takeable proposal, and it doesn't depend on which of the three readings is correct. It only depends on the friend not being unavailable, and on the initiator not already being the person the friend avoids. The original account's uncertainty about whether the avoidance is recent or long-standing is precisely what that framing would begin to resolve.

What I'm actually proposing to take up, and where I'd resist the framing in front of me: I don't accept the objection's reordering, because the readings are not rivals in the way the objection asserts. I do accept the objection's distinction between memorial and normative disagreement, and I'd add that the distinction is internal to the memory reading as well as external to it — a record of a forgotten agreement still leaves the agreement's content to be re-established. I do accept the rival's probe as a low-cost prior, with the caveat that its most likely outcome is uninformative. I don't accept that the material leaves everything undecided; it does decide that the original account's ranked sequence was asserted rather than derived, and that is itself a finding worth preserving rather than softening into 'three plausible readings.'

The one piece of the original account I'd retain unchanged is its own hedge: 'a reading of the material, not a diagnosis of the people.' Everything I've said is a clarification of what that hedge covers. It does not cover the ordering of remedies, which the material does not license, and both successors to the account have grounds to insist on that.
commitments:
Two commitments, and the second is more load-bearing than the first.

First, a claim I'm making and am willing to have count against me: the memory-gap reading, the scope-ambiguity reading, and the avoidance-reading are not three rival candidates for one slot. They're answers to different questions, and only the first two are strictly rivals with each other. If someone shows that in this kind of household the memorial and normative disagreements cannot be separated — that agreeing on what was said and agreeing on what it meant are not two operations — then my sorting collapses back into a single axis, and the objection's framing wins. I've argued against that collapse on conceptual grounds, not empirical ones, and I don't have a case to point to where the separation fails. So this is a commitment with an open vulnerability.

Second, and what I'd actually do next if this is continued: the rival's per-person probe should be run before any record, but with a specific scoring rule stated in advance so that it can't be read post hoc. The rule: if reports cluster around scope, recurrence, or timing, treat the memory and ambiguity readings as both live and proceed to a record as a local trial; if reports do not cluster around those features, treat the probe as returning no finding and do not read non-clustering as support for the standing-negotiation reading. This scoring rule is itself contestable — someone could argue that non-clustering is weakly informative because it makes task-feature disputes less likely — and I'd want that objection on the record before the probe is run, not after. Reason: the rival has already conceded that recollection is in dispute, and I want the probe's interpretation governed by a rule fixed before the results come in.

Third, on what I'm not committing to: I haven't argued that the avoidant friend is being outnumbered, that the household has an unequal load, that a mediator would help, or that the memory reading is false. I also haven't argued that the record-plus-check-in is worse than any alternative, though the rival's insistence that the record may relocate the dispute rather than settle it is a point I've adopted. What I'd resist is the framing that the appropriate response to underdetermination is a wider field of readings; the appropriate response is a narrower question that discriminates, and I've named one. If it returns nothing, I'd rather say so than widen.
